sections.body:
Marriage timing is the question of when to marry. The question has two halves, and they are easy to confuse. One half is the timing of the marriage: the date of the ceremony, the year of the legal form. The other half is the timing of a life: the order in which study, work, a partner, children and money arrive. The second half decides the first, and it is much harder to see.

A date is the visible part. Underneath it sits a **life course** — the sequence of roles and stages that people are expected to move through, and the order in which they usually move through them. A life course describes a pattern in a group of people; it is not a rule for one person. The pattern is written into work, into money, into housing, into what a family expects, and into what the law allows. Next to it sits the **normative timing**: the age, or the stage, at which the milestone is expected. 'Expected' is the important word. The normative timing is what people assume when they do not ask. It is not a rule that something will happen, and it is not a verdict on anybody. It is the point on the clock at which everybody's life is supposed to be at that point, and a person who arrives there later meets a question they never asked.

The error that follows is a comparison of two different systems. A reader whose partner married late compares their own date with a friend who married early, and concludes that one of them is behind. The two dates were produced by different sets of forces: different labour markets, different housing costs, different rules about studying, different families, different laws. The comparison is between the systems, not between the people.

This article gives you the forces that move a date, the words other people use when they talk about timing, and a procedure you can run on your own situation. It does not tell you what to do, and it does not say that one order of events is better than another.
examples: Marriage timing is two questions: when the marriage happens, and when the life does.
A normative timing is what people assume when they do not ask.
Comparing my date with your date compares two systems, not two people.
The date is the visible part; the order of events underneath it is the decision.

sections.body:
A date is the output of a system, and the system has parts. Eight of them do most of the work, and they pull in different directions.

Age pulls in two directions at once: the body and the plan of a life have their own clocks, and people differ in when those clocks say the next part begins. **Education** usually lengthens the road, because more years of study mean later entry to work, later independence and later marriage. That relationship is regular enough to have a name: the **education gradient**. In a group, the further a person goes in schooling, the later the marriage tends to arrive. The gradient is a pattern in a group, and not a cause that works on one person. **Work** and **money** pull together: a wage that covers one household does not cover two, and a job that can disappear cannot carry a mortgage.

Family and **religion** add a second set of expectations. A family has its own timetable for its members, and a religion has rules about the marriage itself: who may marry, in what form, by which ceremony, with whose approval. **Cohabitation** — living together as a couple without being married — moves the timing again, because many couples now share the household first and take the legal form later. **The law** sets the frame around all of it: the age at which a person may marry without a parent's consent, the papers a marriage needs, the registration, the residency rules, and what a divorce later requires. A wedding is a private decision carried out inside a public set of forms, and the forms have their own pace.

The labour market decides how easy it is to be independent at a given age: what a first job pays, whether a contract is stable, whether the cost of housing sits near the wage. Where the forces line up, the marriage comes earlier; where they point the other way, it comes later, and the later pattern is called **deferred marriage**. The move is visible in two numbers. A **mean age** is the total of the ages divided by the number of people. A **median age** is the age in the middle of the list: half the group is older and half is younger. When a few people marry very late, the mean is pulled up and the median stays at the middle of the group, so the two numbers can tell different stories about the same group.
examples: The education gradient is a pattern in a group, not a cause that works on one person.

sections.body:
Four words do most of the work in a conversation about timing, and three of them are used loosely. The first is **postponement**: a planned event moved to a later date. The word is neutral on paper. In a room it is not, because a postponement without a reason sounds like an excuse. Naming the reason — the work, the study, the health, the money — turns it back into a fact.

The second pair is **readiness** and **financial readiness**. Readiness is the whole state: the practical side, the personal side and the relational side. It is a state and not a character, which means it can be there this year and absent the next. Financial readiness is the money part of it: an income that carries two households, savings that survive a bad month, a housing situation that is stable for a while. The two are often confused, and the confusion has a cost. A partner with money and without readiness is told that the money was the point. A partner with readiness and no money is told to wait for money. Ask for the part that is actually missing.

The last word is the **decision horizon**: how far ahead the decision can see. A short horizon — a rent due next month, a contract that ends, a child on the way — pulls the decision towards the present, because the cost of a wrong move is near. A long horizon — a settled income, a house, a plan that covers the next few years — allows the decision to wait. Two people with the same age and the same income can have different horizons, and the gap between two horizons is often the real content of a disagreement about a date.

Note what these four words do not do. None of them is a verdict, and none of them decides anything on its own. They are the words that make the question precise enough to be answered.
examples: The postponement had a reason, and the reason was the contract.
Financial readiness is the money part of readiness; the rest is not a number.

sections.body:
Waiting and marrying early are both trades. Waiting usually buys money, a steadier job, a finished qualification and more certainty about the partner. It also costs time: time as a couple, time for children if children are wanted, and time in which the relationship has to survive the waiting. Marrying early buys shared years, children earlier, a shared budget sooner and a steadier base for a career. It costs money, certainty and preparation, and it can arrive before the person is ready. Neither side of the trade is free, and the two sides do not cancel each other.

The reason to look at the trade-off in the abstract is that it is often invisible in the moment. When people say they are waiting, the wait looks like prudence. When people say they are not waiting, the hurry looks like certainty. Both descriptions are about the mood of a decision, and not about the contents of it.

Two effects sit on top of the trade-off, and both are about the reference group rather than about the couple. **Peer timing** is the timing of the people around you, used as a mirror for your own. It is what people mean by the peer effect, and it sounds from inside like *everybody my age is married*, or *we are the only ones still waiting*. It is a real observation and a weak argument, because the group you compare with may have a different labour market, a different housing situation and a different set of expectations from yours. **Family pressure** is the pressure a family puts on the timing of its members. It is what people mean by the family effect, and it sounds like *when are you going to get married*, or a question about grandchildren asked at a meal. The family is the oldest reference group a person has, and the one with the least interest in your timetable.

Both effects are open to argument, and the argument is not settled. One account says the peer effect is mostly timing: people marry when their own situation allows it, and the group they see is the group whose situation allowed it. Another says it is preference: people marry when the people around them marry, and the group is the cause. The two accounts make different predictions about what happens when a person's circumstances change, and the evidence does not settle between them. What is not in dispute is the practical part. A reference group is a description of other people's arrangements, and it is not a measurement of yours.
examples: Waiting buys stability and costs years; marrying early buys years and costs stability.
Peer timing says everybody my age is married; peer timing is not a measurement of me.
The postponement had a reason, and the reason was the work.
Family pressure asks about grandchildren at the table, and the answer is a plan.

sections.body:
Every reason for a date carries an assumption about the world. The reason is the short sentence. The assumption is the part that has to be true for the sentence to hold. Writing the two apart is the whole use of this table.

Read the reasons for marrying earlier against each other, then the reasons for waiting, then the reasons for not marrying. Notice that the last column is not a list of objections. It is the set of conditions the reason depends on, and most of those conditions can be checked, negotiated, or simply accepted.

A reason that names its own assumption is a strong reason. A reason that hides it is the kind that starts an argument about the wrong thing: about age, about love, about what other people are doing, instead of about the work, the money and the family.
examples: Write the reason, and then write the assumption under it.
Every date comes with a condition attached; say what the condition is.
'We are not ready' is a reason about readiness, and not about age.
A reason that names its own assumption is a strong reason.

sections.body:
Six steps. They take one conversation and an hour of writing, and they work the same for a couple, for a person alone, and for a person who has not decided whether to marry at all. The steps do not produce a date. They produce a plan you can defend, and a point at which you will look again.

The first step separates the practical questions from the social ones, because the two are answered in different places. The practical questions are answered by money, by work, by health, by children, by the law and by the person you are with. The social questions are answered by the people around you, and they are answered by assumption rather than by argument. Mixing the two lists is what makes a date feel like a verdict.

The last two steps are about the conversation. A date is easier to argue about than a life, and it is easier because it is smaller. A conversation about the marriage itself — the ordinary arrangement, the money, the family, the work, the children — is the one that changes the plan. The date follows from that conversation.
examples: First the practical list, then the social list. They are answered in different places.
What has to be true for this to work, and how would I know?
Let us talk about the marriage, and the date will come out of that.
The deadline is my mother's, and I want to say that out loud.
sections.heading: How to work out your own timing
steps: Split the question into two lists. The practical list holds money, work, health, children, the legal and administrative steps, and the partner. The social list holds every voice that has an opinion about the date. Do not solve them together.
Turn each practical item into a condition you can check: what has to be true for this to work, and how you would know. A condition can be true or false; a feeling about the date cannot be checked.
Name the trade-off in one sentence: what you get by waiting, what you give up, and how long you are willing to pay. If the sentence cannot be finished, the reason for waiting is not yet a reason.

Talk about the marriage and not about the date. Say what the shared life would look like on an ordinary Tuesday: the money, the work, the family, the house, the children. Let the date follow from that description.
Agree the plan with the person who will live it, and write it down: the order of events, what each of you expects, and the date you will sit down again and look at the plan.
Say out loud whose deadline it is. If it belongs to your family, your friends, your church or your office, say so. If it belongs to you, say that too, and be ready to say what it is for.

sections.body:
There is no age at which a person is supposed to marry. There is a normative timing, a mean age and a median age, and all three describe a group rather than a threshold. A person who marries before the pattern of the group and a person who marries long after it are reading the same system; they read it at different points.

This article does not judge a decision to marry, to wait, or never to marry. It does not rank the orders of events, and it does not say that one life is fuller than another. The order that works for one person is wrong for another, because the forces are not the same for both.

What it gives you is the forces and the vocabulary. With them you can hear your own situation more clearly, say what you are actually waiting for, and answer a question about your plans without an argument you did not choose. If somebody else is in a hurry about you, the vocabulary is the part that still works.
examples: There is no age at which a person is supposed to marry.
I am waiting for a reason, and the reason is not a date.
This article explains the forces; it does not judge the decision.
The timing is ours, and the explanation is what I can give.
sections.heading: No age is the right age

The first three are for a partner. The next three are for family. The next three are for work. The last three are for a friend who is in a hurry.

The voice is flat on purpose. A sentence about timing that sounds like a verdict starts an argument about the verdict, and the argument moves away from the things that can actually be arranged.
examples: Let us talk about the marriage itself first, and let the date follow from that.

The date is not settled yet, and I will tell you when it is.

sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Marriage timing is not one decision but a set of forces: work, money, study, family, law and the people around you. After reading this you can name the forces that push a date earlier or later, use the vocabulary of timing accurately, tell the peer effect from the family effect, and run a short procedure that separates the practical questions from the pressure.
item.title: The Psychology of Marriage Timing
